17. Checking and recording a study

David Sarrat González

Source: vignettes/book-17-reproduce.Rmd
book-17-reproduce.Rmd

What you will learn

Save a study definition and its data-source information, repeat it at another site, and inspect unsupported cohort rules before running them.

You need: the client packages and the Opal login from Getting started. This chapter uses the two questionnaire sites, omop.questionnaire and omop.questionnaire_site2. They have different education answers and vocabulary dates, so identical recipes need not give identical results.

library(dsOMOPClient)
conns <- ds.omop.login(rep("https://localhost:8443", 2), user = "administrator",
  password = "password",
  server = c("site", "site2"),
  resource = c(site = "omop.questionnaire", site2 = "omop.questionnaire_site2"))$conns

Record the data actually used

Keep the vocabulary and source information returned by these connections. A record for another dataset would not document this study.

vocabularies <- ds.omop.vocab.vocabularies(conns = conns)$per_site
sources <- ds.omop.cdm.source(conns = conns)$per_site
vocabulary_rows <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(vocabularies), function(site) {
  x <- vocabularies[[site]]
  x <- x[x$vocabulary_id == "Questionnaire", c("vocabulary_id", "vocabulary_version"), drop = FALSE]
  data.frame(Site = site, x)
}))
vocabulary_rows
Site vocabulary_id vocabulary_version
site Questionnaire 2025-01-01
site2 Questionnaire 2026-01-01 
source_rows <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(sources), function(site)
  data.frame(Site = site, sources[[site]][c("cdm_source_name", "cdm_version", "source_release_date")])))
source_rows
Site cdm_source_name cdm_version source_release_date
site Synthetic questionnaire dataset 5.4 2025-01-01
site2 Synthetic questionnaire dataset 5.4 2025-01-01

The questionnaire vocabulary dates are 2025-01-01 and 2026-01-01. Retain both: newer wording can change labels even when concept IDs stay the same. Both source records identify the synthetic questionnaire dataset, CDM 5.4 and a source release date of 2025-01-01; these fields identify what the study record saves.

Define and inspect the study

Education question 900001 was found in chapter 4. Include education so that a repeated run can reveal differences between sites. Death year is an ordered calendar category; age is completed age at death.

education <- omop_variable(event = omop_event("observation", 900001L),
  reducer = omop_reduce("last_value", value = "value_as_concept_id"))
check <- omop_recipe(variables = list(education = education,
  age = omop_age_at("death"),
  death_period = omop_date("death", omop_date_spec(precision = "year"))),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
result <- recipe_execute(check, out = c(people = "D_documented"), conns = conns["site"])
published <- recipe_codebook(result)
published[[1]]$columns[c("name", "semantic_type", "r_type", "unit")]
name semantic_type r_type unit
person_id key character not_applicable
education concept factor not_applicable
age numeric integer years
death_period date ordered_factor not_applicable

Read r_type: age is numeric, while education and death period are factors. Keep this codebook to interpret the assigned columns later; it does not report how many people have missing values.

Save the study record

The recipe stores the selection rules. Its explanation makes those rules readable, and its digest identifies the definition. Save the codebook, software information, and both sites’ source metadata alongside it. These files contain definitions and metadata, not patient rows.

record_dir <- "questionnaire-study"
dir.create(record_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
recipe_save(check, file.path(record_dir, "recipe.json"))
explanation <- recipe_explain(check)
writeLines(explanation$text, file.path(record_dir, "explanation.txt"))
writeLines(explanation$digest, file.path(record_dir, "plan-digest.txt"))
saveRDS(published, file.path(record_dir, "codebook-site.rds"))
saveRDS(vocabularies, file.path(record_dir, "vocabularies.rds"))
saveRDS(sources, file.path(record_dir, "sources.rds"))
package_versions <- vapply(c("dsOMOPClient", "DSI", "dsBaseClient"),
  function(p) as.character(packageVersion(p)), character(1))
write.csv(data.frame(Package = names(package_versions), Release = unname(package_versions)),
  file.path(record_dir, "client-packages.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
saveRDS(ds.omop.server.version(conns = conns), file.path(record_dir, "server-packages.rds"))
list.files(record_dir)
#> [1] "client-packages.csv" "codebook-site.rds"   "explanation.txt"
#> [4] "plan-digest.txt"     "recipe.json"         "server-packages.rds"
#> [7] "sources.rds"         "vocabularies.rds"

The filenames identify the definition, software and data sources needed to repeat the study. Matching digests establish matching rules; they cannot establish that a database has stayed unchanged.

Run the saved definition at the second site 

restored <- recipe_load(file.path(record_dir, "recipe.json"))
second_result <- recipe_execute(restored, out = c(people = "D_repeated"), conns = conns["site2"])
saveRDS(recipe_codebook(second_result), file.path(record_dir, "codebook-site2.rds"))
dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_repeated$death_period",
  useNA = "always", datasources = conns["site2"])$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_repeated$death_period
#> 2023 2024   NA
#>   18   18   12

The second site has 18 deaths in 2023, 18 in 2024, and 12 people without a death year. The counts describe its data; the saved recipe describes how those categories were obtained.

Exercises

1. Compare data, not just definitions. Tabulate education at each site after the separate runs. What changed?

Solution 1

dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_documented$education",
  useNA = "always", datasources = conns["site"])$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_documented$education
#>  Secondary education University education                   NA
#>                   12                   12                   24
dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_repeated$education",
  useNA = "always", datasources = conns["site2"])$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_repeated$education
#> University qualification                       NA
#>                       24                       24

Site has 12 Secondary and 12 University answers; site2 has 24 University answers. Both have 24 missing answers. The newer catalogue calls University education “University qualification”. Because these were separate executions, their labels were resolved separately; a joint execution reconciles them as shown in chapter 10.

2. Inspect an unsupported cohort rule. Circe JSON describes an OHDSI cohort. Does a successful strict import establish the intended clinical meaning?

Solution 2

circe_json <- jsonlite::toJSON(list(AdditionalCriteria = list(Type = "ALL",
  CriteriaList = list(list(unsupported = TRUE)))), auto_unbox = TRUE)
circe_check <- recipe_circe_check(circe_json)
circe_check$issues[c("path", "remedy")]
path remedy
$.AdditionalCriteria AdditionalCriteria has no implemented adapter; retain the complete definition.
$.PrimaryCriteria Provide an object with the documented structural fields.

The check identifies structural problems in this example, so it is not ready for extraction. Attempt the strict import and read its refusal:

recipe_import_circe(circe_json)
#> Error:
#> ! unsupported_circe_construct: $.AdditionalCriteria; AdditionalCriteria has no implemented adapter; retain the complete definition. Inspect recipe_circe_check() for all structural issues.

unsupported_circe_construct identifies the unsupported AdditionalCriteria rule. Keep the complete cohort definition and implement that rule in a reviewed native recipe before extracting. A successful strict import means every construct had an adapter; you must still compare the translated population with the intended inclusion and exclusion rules. Never delete a scientific criterion merely to make an import succeed.

3. Read the actual calendar levels. Which years can the assigned death-period column represent, and are they ordered?

Solution 3

columns <- recipe_codebook(result)[[1]]$columns
period <- match("death_period", columns$name)
data.frame(Year = columns$levels[[period]]$labels,
  Type = columns$r_type[[period]])
Year Type
2023 ordered_factor
2024 ordered_factor

The levels are 2023 and 2024 in chronological order. A column called “year” could instead be numeric or a Date under a different declaration; its name alone is insufficient.

Exercise 4: preserve a required clean period

A prebuilt analysis is a named catalogue procedure that returns an aggregate; a recipe instead lets you choose populations, variables and output tables. Each analysis declares its supported settings, so inspect its definition with ds.omop.analysis.get() before using it for a study.

For a small successful example, the person-count analysis needs no settings:

person_counts <- ds.omop.analysis.run("dsomop:demo.person_count_by_gender",
  conns = conns["site"])
person_counts$pooled[c("gender_name", "n_persons")]
gender_name n_persons
MALE 25
FEMALE 20

The default run describes all people at this site. Its male count of 25 and female count of 20 are rounded down to five-person bands: 25–29 and 20–24, respectively. They are not exact counts to sum for a study denominator.

The incidence-rate analysis is a different catalogue procedure: it describes first-episode incidence over a follow-up window, with no clean period by default. Suppose a study requires 365 observed days without the outcome before entry. Can the incidence-rate analysis below implement that requirement? If it refuses, which scientific rule must the alternative preserve?

Solution: keep the outcome-free observation period

ds.omop.analysis.run("dsomop:incidence.rate",
  params = list(clean_window = 365), conns = conns)
#> Error:
#> ! unsupported_clean_window: params.clean_window; zero selects the descriptive first-episode/full-window estimand; use a validated native risk recipe when a clean period is required

unsupported_clean_window means this analysis cannot implement the required clean period. Preserve continuous prior observation, the outcome-free period and the specified follow-up in a reviewed recipe. The population lessons and drug comparison show the relevant rules; setting the clean period to zero would change the scientific question.

Recap

Keep the rules, codebook, software and actual source metadata together. Repeating a definition at another site is an opportunity to check data differences, not a reason to assume identical answers.
